1959 Piaggio Vespa 400 Is Not a Scooter, but a Rare Microcar
14 photos
Photo: eBay/Premier Auto Group of South Florida
Built by Piaggio, the Vespa is perhaps the world's most iconic scooter brand. First introduced in 1946, the Vespa scooter is still around today, retaining the design that made the original popular. But did you know that the Vespa badge also found its way on a car?
It happened in 1957, when Piaggio joined the microcar market. The first microcars emerged in the years following World War II, with several companies jumping on the bandwagon in the early 1950s. By 1953, Iso had debuted the Isetta, which was later licensed by BMW, while Messerschmitt had launched the KR175. The Fuldamobil was introduced in 1950.
Piaggio reportedly started working on its microcar in 1952, but the production model didn't arrive until 1957, the same year when Fiat launched the more iconic 500. Piaggio called it the Vespa 400. But unlike the scooter, the microcar was produced by ACMA in France.
Smaller but just as charming as the Fiat 500 , the Vespa 400 was shaped like a two-door sedan and measured only 112 inches (2,850 mm) long. The 66.7-inch (1,693 mm) wheelbase provided room for two seats, but the passenger cabin could also accommodate two small children on the optional cushion. The tiny vehicle tipped the scales at only 790 pounds (360 kg).
Unsurprisingly, the Vespa 400 was fitted with a two-stroke two-cylinder engine. The 400cc engine delivered 13 horsepower in its early configuration, with output increased to 14 horsepower later on. The microcar was able to reach up to 55 mph (89 kph).
The Vespa 400 was pretty popular at first, selling 12,130 units in 1958. However, sales dropped to around 8,700 examples in 1959 and declined dramatically in 1960. Piaggio discontinued the model in 1961, with a total production of nearly 31,000 units. Most of these cars were sold in France. Nearly 1,700 examples crossed the pond to the United States.
The Vespa 400 is quite rare today, as most of these microcars were abandoned in disrepair. Restored examples are hard to come by, which is why this 1959 Vespa that surfaced in Pompano Beach, Florida, is a spectacular find.
For sale via Premier Auto Group, this Piaggio was restored about 10 years ago. The Narvik Blue paint is flawless, while the interior, albeit very sparse, is factory correct and amazingly clean.
Interestingly, this Vespa 400 wasn't sold in the US. The vehicle was actually delivered new in France and made the trip to North America sometime later. There's no info on whether it was restored before or after it made it into the US. The car has a four-speed manual gearbox, which was only available in European markets. This Vespa 400 is technically a GT model.
How much to take this tiny two-seater home? The dealership is asking $37,500 , but it's also accepting offers. It may sound like a lot for such a small vehicle, but some examples have actually fetched more at public auction in recent years.
The most expensive Vespa 400 changed hands for the equivalent of $42,000 in 2020. Back in 2011, another one sold for $41,250 at Amelia Island. In 2025, a 1959 version like this one traded for $40,320 in Arizona.
